title: How fast
hook: in the commentaries, many mind-moments pass while one moment of matter lasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body's matter: sense doors, the life faculty, and the heat and food that keep a living body being made. Your line: living matter. Did you check your hands' warmth at a meal? Day one thousand eighty-four.

There's a short passage in the Buddha's discourses that sounds almost like a shrug. He says he can't think of anything that changes as quickly as the mind. So quickly, he adds, that it isn't easy to find a comparison for it. That's the whole teaching. No number, no measurement, just a teacher admitting that the mind outruns his similes. The Abhidhamma and its commentaries didn't leave it there. They tried to measure it anyway. Today, how fast.
screen: `NOTHING CHANGES SO QUICKLY.` → `HARD TO FIND A SIMILE.` → `THEY TRIED TO MEASURE IT.`

segments.voice: Start with the smallest unit. In the Abhidhamma, a moment of mind, a khana, has three phases: it arises, it stands, it dissolves. Then the next one arises. In this picture, nothing in between holds still long enough to be a self watching from the side. Each moment does its one job and is gone. Now set matter beside it. Matter, the manual says, also arises and passes, but more slowly. And here's the measure that gives today its name: one moment of matter, the manual says, lasts as long as seventeen moments of mind. So while a single moment of matter in your hand comes and goes, a whole run of mental moments has already arisen, seen, felt, and vanished. Now set a blink beside that. In the time it takes the eyelids to close and open, tradition says, a great many mind-moments pass. Some later teachers reach for huge numbers to make the point, and those numbers can be held loosely. The point isn't the arithmetic. It's the direction. Whatever you call your experience of this second is already a crowd of moments, each one gone before you could name it. Why would a teaching bother to measure this? Because of the Buddha's shrug. If nothing changes as quickly as the mind, then nothing you're feeling right now is going to stay. A sharp word, a craving, a wave of fear: by the time you've noticed it, it's already becoming something else. The speed isn't meant to make you dizzy. It's meant to loosen the grip.
screen: `ARISE, STAND, DISSOLVE.` · `MATTER LASTS SEVENTEEN MIND-MOMENTS.` · `A BLINK IS A CROWD OF MOMENTS.` · then, large: `THE SPEED LOOSENS THE GRIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: blink, and notice. Sit easily with your eyes open, resting on something nearby. Then blink once, slowly on purpose. Notice the light going, the dark, the light returning. Notice that the thing you were looking at seems to be waiting there, unchanged. Then rest, eyes open or closed, and let the breath carry you. Each time you remember, blink once more and watch the whole small drama happen. The bell holds the time.
How fast. In the manual, one moment of matter lasts while seventeen moments of mind arise and pass, and a blink holds a great many. Today's word.

Your line: faster than a blink. Today, the next time a feeling hits hard, blink once, slowly, and notice whether the feeling on the other side of the blink is quite the same. Day one thousand eighty-four.

howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the three phases of a mind-moment and the manual's comparison of mind-moments to moments of matter, and some meditation teachers in the Theravada tradition guide students to notice how quickly experience changes.

pairs: hard to find a simile for the mind

myth: in the Abhidhamma, matter changes faster than mind
the other way round: one moment of matter lasts seventeen moments of mind.
the Buddha said it isn't easy to find a simile for how fast the mind changes
in a short passage of the discourses; the Abhidhamma tried to measure it anyway.
the huge numbers in the commentaries are the point of the teaching
the direction matters more than the arithmetic: nothing felt now is going to stay.

fork.setup: you blink, and the room is still there, apparently unchanged. by the manual's account, what happened during the blink?
options: a great many mind-moments arose and passed
fork.reveal: tradition says a great many mind-moments pass in a blink; whatever you call this second is already a crowd of moments.

original.note: Pali: a moment, the smallest unit of mind, which arises, stands and dissolves.

trapdoor: what you thought: the mind changes its mind a lot.
what it means: a mind-moment arises, stands and dissolves, and one moment of matter lasts seventeen of them.
what a scholar hears: the sutta passage says only that nothing changes as quickly as the mind; the seventeen-moment count comes from the manual.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1.48, nothing changes as quickly as the mind
Abhidhammattha Sangaha IV (cognitive process), three phases of a mind-moment and the seventeen-moment lifespan of matter
Abhidhammattha Sangaha VI (Compendium of Matter), the arising and passing of matter

notes: AN 1.48 paraphrased (numbering varies by edition; some count it AN 1.48, others AN I.10). Confirm reference and wording.
Three phases (uppada, thiti, bhanga) and 'one moment of matter lasts seventeen mind-moments' stated from Abhidhammattha Sangaha IV/VI; confirm.

'In a blink a great many mind-moments pass': the commentaries give very large figures (e.g. for a lightning flash or the snap of a finger); the script gives no figure and invites the listener to hold such numbers loosely. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with that framing.
The Sautrantika and other schools held different views on momentariness; not raised here (day 1091 covers another school).
